evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with depression: recognition, severity grading, risk, first-line treatment, antidepressant use and withdrawal, lithium and antipsychotic augmentation, non-response, relapse prevention. Verified against NICE NG222 and FDA labels; no Saudi guideline found; SFDA not checked.
findings: NICE NG222 recommendations, Table 1 and Table 2 were read in full on 13 Oct 2026; doses and contraindications were read from US FDA labels via openFDA on the same date.
NG222 is a UK guideline; its service and legal references (NHS, Mental Health Act 2007, ECTAS) do not apply in Saudi Arabia.
unverifiedSections: SFDA registration of the antidepressants and lithium not checked (the SFDA site refused automated access from the authoring environment)
No Saudi depression guideline was found; none is cited
ICD-11 or DSM-5 diagnostic criteria are referred to by NG222 but not reproduced
Pathophysiology beyond the points in NG222 is not covered because the recommendations do not describe it
The sertraline FDA label read is version 2 from November 2019 and may be superseded
Doses for antipsychotics, mirtazapine, trazodone, lamotrigine and liothyronine are not given because no label was read for them
Mental health legislation and ECT accreditation requirements apply to the UK, not Saudi Arabia

pathophysiology.summary: Depression covers many different mental health problems marked by loss of positive affect (loss of interest and enjoyment), low mood and associated emotional, cognitive, physical and behavioural symptoms. NICE NG222 describes severity as a continuum made of symptoms, duration and impact on personal and social functioning, and groups new episodes as less severe or more severe. This topic covers adults only.
keyMechanisms: Severity is a consequence of three elements together: symptoms (frequency and intensity), duration of the disorder, and impact on personal and social functioning (NICE NG222, Definitions of depression and severity).

Less severe depression covers subthreshold and mild depression; more severe depression covers moderate and severe depression; a PHQ-9 score below 16 was used for less severe and 16 or more for more severe (NICE NG222, Definitions of depression and severity).

Development, course and severity can be affected by past depression, coexisting disorders, mood elevation history, previous treatment response, relationships, lifestyle, stressful or traumatic events, living conditions, substance use, debt, employment and isolation (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.7).

Risk of relapse is higher with recurrent episodes (especially frequent or within 2 years), incomplete earlier response with residual symptoms, unhelpful coping such as avoidance and rumination, past severe depression, other chronic physical or mental health problems, and persisting contributing factors (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.8.2).

references.title: NICE NG222: Depression in adults: treatment and management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 29 June 2022 (no later update date shown on the page opened), Definitions of depression and severity; Recommendations 1.2.7 and 1.8.2

symptoms: Feeling down, depressed or hopeless, and little interest or pleasure in doing things, over the last month (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.1).
Associated emotional, cognitive, physical and behavioural symptoms; low mood and loss of interest and enjoyment are the core (NICE NG222, Definitions).
Functional, interpersonal and social difficulties (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.3).
Suicidal ideation or self-harm, which must be asked about directly (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.8).
Anxiety symptoms, which commonly accompany depression (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.13).
physicalSigns: NG222 does not describe examination signs; assessment is by mental state review and functional impact (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.3 and 1.2.6).
Not eating or drinking because of the depression marks life-threatening illness and is an example in which a rapid response is needed (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.13.1).
Psychotic symptoms such as unusual thought content and hallucinations (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.12.4).
redFlags: Considerable immediate risk to self or others: refer urgently to specialist mental health services (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.9).
Suicide risk: do not withhold treatment, limit the amount of medicine available if needed, increase support and consider specialist referral (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.12).
Depression with psychotic symptoms: offer referral to specialist mental health services (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.12.1).
History of mood elevation raises the possibility of bipolar disorder (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.7).
Marked or prolonged agitation in the early stages of treatment: review treatment (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.10).
precipitants: Stressful or traumatic life events such as redundancy, divorce, bereavement or trauma (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.7).
Past history of depression, or a chronic physical health problem with functional impairment (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.1).
Drug and alcohol use, debt, unemployment, loneliness and social isolation (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.7).
Winter depression following a seasonal pattern (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.39).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Any history of mood elevation; ask when assessing for depression (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.7). Manage using the NICE bipolar disorder guideline.

differentials.condition: Anxiety disorder with comorbid depressive symptoms
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: When there is an anxiety disorder with depressive symptoms, consult guidance for that disorder and consider treating the anxiety disorder first; when depression is accompanied by anxiety symptoms, usually treat the depression first (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.13).
Unusual thought content or hallucinations; needs specialist referral (NICE NG222 Recs 1.12.1 and 1.12.4).
Coexisting personality disorder; treatment for depression is not withheld because of it (NICE NG222 Recs 1.11.1–1.11.4).

differentials.condition: Depression in a person with an acquired cognitive impairment or dementia
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Be aware of any acquired cognitive impairment during assessment and adjust delivery of interventions (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.14–1.2.15).
Symptoms that significantly impair personal and social functioning over a long period, sometimes never treated before (NICE NG222 Recs 1.10.1–1.10.2).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: A yes to either question: during the last month, often bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless; or by little interest or pleasure in doing things
PHQ-9 below 16: less severe depression; PHQ-9 16 or more: more severe depression (used as an indicator alongside clinical judgement, not a symptom count alone, Rec. 1.2.6)
NG222 refers to the ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria for depression and does not reproduce them

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Review after starting treatment (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.3 and 1.4.11)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Review 2 to 4 weeks after starting; medication review usually within 2 weeks, or at 1 week for people aged 18 to 25 or with particular suicide concern

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: No response to treatment (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.1)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: No response after 4 weeks of antidepressant at a recognised therapeutic dose, or after 4 to 6 weeks of psychological therapy or combined treatment

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Medication duration (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11 and Table 2)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Antidepressant typically at least 6 months, including after symptoms remit
Review at least every 6 months while continuing antidepressant for relapse prevention
Plasma lithium not above 1.0 mmol/L; usually at or above 0.4 mmol/L for augmentation, 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L for age 65 or above

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Yes to either question about low mood or loss of interest in the last month.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Ask people who may have depression, especially with past depression or a chronic physical illness with functional impairment; if positive, review mental state and functional, interpersonal and social difficulties, or refer if not competent to assess (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.1–1.2.3).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: PHQ-9 of 16 or more indicates more severe depression; below 16 less severe.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Consider a validated measure when assessing, to inform and evaluate treatment; consider routine outcome monitoring at follow-up. It does not replace a full assessment (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.4, 1.2.6 and 1.4.3).
ruleIn.normalValue: NG222 gives no 'normal' PHQ-9 value; the only stated threshold is 16

references.title: NICE NG222: Depression in adults: treatment and management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 29 June 2022 (no later update date shown on the page opened), Recommendations 1.9.1–1.9.2

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise, assess and manage risk
actions: Ask the two identification questions in people who may have depression (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.1); if positive and competent to assess, review mental state and functional, interpersonal and social difficulties (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.3).
Do a full assessment that does not rely on a symptom count: severity, history, duration, course and functional impairment (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.6).
Always ask directly about suicidal ideation and intent (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.8).
Refer urgently to specialist mental health services if there is considerable immediate risk to self or others (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.9).
If at risk of suicide, do not withhold treatment; consider overdose toxicity and limit the quantity supplied if needed; consider more frequent contact (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.12).

clinicalManagement.title: Classify severity and agree a treatment
actions: Discuss the person's views, past experience and preferences and agree a treatment together; people can decline treatment (NICE NG222 Recs 1.3.1, 1.3.3 and 1.5.2).
Use the least intrusive and most resource-efficient treatment appropriate to need, or one that worked before (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.2).
Review progress 2 to 4 weeks after starting any treatment; check adherence, side effects and suicidal ideation (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.3).

All Table 1 options can be first line, starting with the least intrusive, guided self-help; others are group CBT or behavioural activation, individual CBT or behavioural activation, group exercise, group mindfulness, interpersonal psychotherapy, counselling, short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy and SSRIs (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.5.2 and Table 1).
Do not routinely offer an antidepressant first line; offer it only if that is the person's informed preference (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.5.3).
If the person does not want treatment or is improving, arrange further assessment normally within 2 to 4 weeks (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.5.1).

All Table 2 options can be first line: combined individual CBT and an antidepressant, individual CBT, individual behavioural activation, antidepressant medication, problem-solving, counselling, short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, interpersonal psychotherapy, guided self-help and group exercise (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.6.1 and Table 2).
SSRIs are generally well tolerated and should be the first choice of antidepressant for most people (NICE NG222 Table 2).
Consider behavioural couples therapy, 15 to 20 sessions over 5 to 6 months (NICE NG222 Recs 1.7.1–1.7.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Antidepressant prescribing and safety
actions: Agree a plan covering reasons, choices, dose, benefits, side effects and withdrawal effects, and give written information (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.10).
Explain that benefit is usually seen within 4 weeks, treatment may need to continue at least 6 months after remission, and first review is usually within 2 weeks (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11).

For age 18 to 25 or increased suicide risk: assess mental state before starting, review 1 week after starting or increasing the dose, then review no later than 4 weeks after the start (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.22).
Do not routinely start tricyclics other than lofepramine in people at significant suicide risk, because of overdose toxicity (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.23).
In older people, consider physical health and interactions, monitor side effects, and be alert to falls, fractures and hyponatraemia (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.24).
Do not prescribe or advise St John's Wort for depression (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.38).

clinicalManagement.title: No or limited response
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From 4 weeks of medication or 4 to 6 weeks of therapy
actions: First discuss contributing personal, social, environmental or physical factors, and adherence problems, then make a shared decision (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.1).
If still no response, review the diagnosis and consider alternative or comorbid conditions; reassure that other treatments can work (NICE NG222 Recs 1.9.2–1.9.3).

branches.condition: Limited response to psychological therapy alone
actions: Switch to another psychological treatment, add an SSRI, or switch to an SSRI alone (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.4).

Add group exercise, switch to a psychological therapy, increase the dose within the licensed range if tolerated, switch within or across class, or combine psychological therapy with medication (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.5).
Higher doses may not be more effective and can increase side effects; monitor after dose increases (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.5).
Switch psychological therapy, increase the dose or switch antidepressant, or add another medication (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.6).

Explain the added side-effect burden and consider specialist referral. Options include adding an antidepressant of a different class such as mirtazapine or trazodone, a second-generation antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, lithium, ECT, lamotrigine or liothyronine (NICE NG222 Recs 1.9.8–1.9.9).
Avoid dangerous combinations such as an SSRI, SNRI or tricyclic with an MAOI (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Psychotic, chronic and severe depression
actions: Psychotic depression: offer specialist referral; consider an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic such as olanzapine or quetiapine (NICE NG222 Recs 1.12.1–1.12.2).
Consider ECT for severe depression if the person prefers it, a rapid response is needed (for example not eating or drinking), or other treatments have failed (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.13.1).

Chronic depressive symptoms with significant impairment: CBT, SSRI, SNRI, tricyclic, or CBT with an SSRI or tricyclic; CBT should address avoidance, rumination and interpersonal difficulties (NICE NG222 Recs 1.10.2–1.10.3).
Do not withhold treatment because of a coexisting personality disorder (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.11.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Stopping medication and preventing relapse
actions: Discuss that continuing treatment after remission may lower relapse risk, and the risks of long-term antidepressants (NICE NG222 Recs 1.8.1 and 1.8.3).

For higher relapse risk after antidepressant-only remission, consider continuing the medication at the dose that led to remission, group CBT or mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, or both (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.8.5).
Review at least every 6 months while continuing, using a validated rating scale (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.8.11).

To stop an antidepressant, reduce the dose in steps (for example 50% of the previous dose, then smaller reductions such as 25%); take more care with paroxetine and venlafaxine, and for fluoxetine 20 mg a day alternate-day dosing can be a suitable reduction (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.16 and 1.4.18).
Explain that withdrawal symptoms are not relapse; for more severe withdrawal consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.19–1.4.21).

regimens.dose: 50 mg once daily initially; may be increased up to 200 mg/day (FDA label)
regimens.duration: At least 6 months, including after symptoms remit (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11)
adjustments: Dose changes should not occur at intervals under 1 week (FDA label)
NICE advises increasing within the licensed range only if tolerated, because higher doses may not be more effective (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.5)
monitoring: Review within 2 weeks, or at 1 week for age 18 to 25 or suicide concern (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11)
Hyponatraemia, bleeding risk and sexual function effects (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.24 and 1.8.3)
contraindications: MAOI within 14 days before or after, or linezolid or IV methylene blue (FDA label section on contraindications)
Hypersensitivity to sertraline or any inactive ingredient

regimens.dose: 10 mg once daily; maximum 20 mg once daily (FDA label section 2.1)
regimens.duration: At least 6 months, including after symptoms remit (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11)
adjustments: Increase to 20 mg after at least 1 week if needed (FDA label section 2.1)
Elderly patients and hepatic impairment: 10 mg once daily (FDA label section 2.4)
A fixed-dose trial did not show greater benefit of 20 mg over 10 mg (FDA label section 2.1)
monitoring: ECG monitoring when combined with an antipsychotic in people with cardiovascular risk, because escitalopram can prolong the QT interval (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.34)
contraindications: MAOI within 14 days, linezolid or IV methylene blue
Hypersensitivity to escitalopram or citalopram (FDA label section 4)

regimens.indication: Depression not responding to an antidepressant, augmentation (specialist advice)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with depression and limited response
regimens.dose: Dose set by response, tolerability and plasma level: not above 1.0 mmol/L, usually at or above 0.4 mmol/L for augmentation (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.28); the FDA label starting dose of 300 mg three times daily is for bipolar I disorder, not depression
regimens.duration: Stop only in specialist mental health services or on their advice, reducing gradually over 1 to 3 months (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.32)
adjustments: Levels 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L for age 65 or above (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.28)
FDA label: avoid if creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min; start lower and titrate slowly if 30 to 89 mL/min (section 2.5)
monitoring: Plasma level 12 hours post dose, 1 week after starting and after each dose change, weekly until stable, every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months (every 3 months in older people, interacting drugs, renal or thyroid risk, poor control, poor adherence, or last level 0.8 mmol/L or higher) (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.27)
Weight, renal and thyroid function and calcium at least every 6 months (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.25)
Signs of toxicity: diarrhoea, vomiting, coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion and convulsions (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.28)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to an inactive ingredient (FDA label section 4)
Boxed warning: lithium toxicity can occur at doses close to therapeutic concentrations
ACE inhibitors, angiotensin 2 receptor blockers, diuretics and NSAIDs can change lithium levels (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.28)

medicationPlan.note: NG222 names classes and examples but gives few doses, so sertraline and escitalopram doses come from US FDA labels; lithium use in depression is augmentation outside the FDA label's bipolar I indication. Check SFDA registration, the Saudi formulary and local shared-care arrangements.

learningObjectives: Recognise depression with the two identification questions and grade it as less or more severe.
Match first-line treatment to severity and preference, and manage suicide risk.
Monitor antidepressants, recognise non-response and stop medication safely.
keyPoints: PHQ-9 below 16 is less severe; 16 or more is more severe; use clinical assessment, not scores alone.
Do not routinely offer an antidepressant first line for less severe depression.
Review 2 to 4 weeks after starting; at 1 week for age 18 to 25 or suicide concern.
Lithium and antipsychotic augmentation need baseline tests, scheduled monitoring and shared care.
Antidepressants are reduced in stages; withdrawal symptoms are not relapse.
pitfalls: Relying on a symptom count or score without functional and history assessment (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.6).
Withholding treatment because of suicide risk or a personality disorder (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.12 and 1.11.1).
Starting a tricyclic other than lofepramine in a person at significant suicide risk (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.23).
Raising a dose repeatedly when higher doses may not add benefit (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.9.5).
Stopping an antidepressant abruptly or reading withdrawal as relapse (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.16 and 1.4.19).
Advising St John's Wort (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.38).

patientEducation: Give up-to-date written and verbal information suited to language and culture (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.1.2).
Explain early effects of antidepressants, the 4-week time to benefit, the first review date and the need to continue for at least 6 months after remission (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.11).

Advise the person and family or carers to watch for mood change, agitation, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts, especially when starting or changing treatment, and to make contact (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.2.11).
Explain withdrawal symptoms and to talk to the prescriber before stopping (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.12–1.4.14).
Give lithium users safe-use information (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.31).
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular physical activity such as walking, swimming or gardening, ideally outdoors, may improve wellbeing (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.40).
A healthy diet, limiting alcohol and enough sleep may help wellbeing (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.41).
mdtReferrals: Specialist mental health services for considerable immediate risk, psychotic symptoms, or complex or resistant depression (NICE NG222 Recs 1.2.9, 1.10.8 and 1.12.1).
Psychological therapy services for CBT, behavioural activation, interpersonal therapy, counselling, mindfulness or psychodynamic therapy (NICE NG222 Tables 1 and 2).
Specialist-supervised or shared-care arrangements for lithium and antipsychotic augmentation (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.29 and 1.4.35).
dischargeCriteria: NG222 sets no discharge criteria; remission with a relapse-prevention plan and agreed follow-up is the aim (NICE NG222 Recs 1.8.1 and 1.8.4).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review 2 to 4 weeks after starting treatment, then as the plan sets; those continuing an antidepressant for relapse prevention are reviewed at least every 6 months (NICE NG222 Recs 1.4.3 and 1.8.11). People who stop an antidepressant are monitored for withdrawal and return of symptoms (NICE NG222 Rec. 1.4.17).

guidelineComparison.title: Lithium plasma-level targets: NICE NG222 (depression augmentation) vs FDA label (bipolar I disorder)

values: Not above 1.0 mmol/L; usually at or above 0.4 mmol/L; 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L for age 65 or above (Rec. 1.4.28)
Acute mania or mixed episodes 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L; maintenance 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L (section 2.2)
12 hours post dose, 1 week after starting, then weekly until stable (Rec. 1.4.27)
After 3 days, 12 hours after the last dose, then regularly until stable (section 2.2)
Monitor more often with significant renal impairment (Rec. 1.4.25)
Avoid if creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min; start lower in 30 to 89 mL/min (section 2.5)

guidelineComparison.note: The two sources address different conditions (augmentation in depression versus bipolar I disorder); the units mmol/L and mEq/L are numerically equal for lithium. Specialist advice decides the individual target.
